introduction_strategy.hook_hypothesis: Recent literature evaluates neural reasoning capabilities on combinatorial grid puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme, arguing that recurrent neural networks and classical energy formulations learn underlying reasoning dynamics.
introduction_strategy.problem_gap_hypothesis: While specialized classical energy models report near-instantaneous training and frontier LLMs utilize massive token-budget chains of thought, there is no standardized, small-budget benchmark comparing direct LLM autoregressive reasoning, LLM-synthesized deterministic solvers, and energy-based models on identical test puzzles under strict cost, latency, and reliability constraints.

related_work_strategy.overview: Examine two primary methodology paradigms preceding our study: looped/recurrent energy-based constraint satisfaction models and large language model chain-of-thought reasoning for algorithmic tasks.

subsections.subsection_title: 2.2 Large Language Models: Direct Reasoning vs. Program Synthesis
subsections.sota_investigation_mission: Identify studies evaluating frontier LLMs on exact algorithmic reasoning, contrasting internal chain-of-thought inference against program-aided or tool-augmented problem solving.
subsections.limitation_hypothesis: Direct autoregressive chain-of-thought for exact combinatorial satisfaction is prone to context-window exhaustion and subtle constraint violations, rendering it orders of magnitude more expensive and less reliable than synthesizing an external program.

Program synthesis vs chain of thought discrete reasoning accuracy
subsections.bridge_to_our_method: We empirically benchmark direct chain-of-thought generation against one-shot standard-library Python solver synthesis across Claude 5.5 series models on identical Sudoku-Extreme test samples.

content_bullets: State the emerging debate over whether looped neural models and frontier LLMs learn true reasoning on combinatorial benchmarks like Sudoku-Extreme.

Outline our comparative evaluation across three paradigms on 500 Sudoku-Extreme test puzzles on a single laptop CPU ($3.75 total API spend): direct LLM thinking, LLM-synthesized Python backtracking solvers, and an independent CPU re-implementation of CRAM (learned and hand-set energy models).

Highlight core quantitative results: direct LLM reasoning is slow (105-166 s median), costly ($0.014-$0.426/puzzle), and prone to token exhaustion or hallucinations; one-shot LLM-generated code achieves 100% accuracy (4,500/4,500 puzzle runs) at 1.0-1.8 ms per puzzle; CRAM reproduces near-perfect solve rates (496-497/500) with perfect peer recovery (1.000), but a hand-set single-weight energy matches learned performance (497/500).
Conclude that programmatic tool synthesis is the most reliable and cost-effective approach for frontier LLMs, confirming that Sudoku success does not necessarily demonstrate learned reasoning.
Introduce the use of Sudoku-Extreme as a benchmark for claims regarding emergent reasoning in recurrent neural architectures and foundation models.
Describe the recent introduction of CRAM (Hoover et al., 2026), which reports 99.996% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme in 42 ms of GPU training.
Contrast this with common industrial practices where frontier LLMs are prompted to solve complex puzzles directly via extended chain-of-thought.
Establish an honest, small-budget, single-machine experimental comparison on 500 test puzzles from sapientinc/sudoku-extreme.
Demonstrate that direct LLM chain-of-thought reasoning is expensive, slow, and unreliable, hitting token ceilings on extreme puzzles.
Show that prompt-synthesized Python backtracking solvers achieve 100% success across 9 independent solvers from three model tiers at sub-2 millisecond latency per puzzle.
Provide an independent CPU re-implementation of CRAM demonstrating 1.000 constraint peer recovery, while confirming that a zero-training hand-set energy achieves identical accuracy.

subsections.subsection_title: 2.1 Classical Energy Models and Neural Solvers
content_bullets: Review Hopfield-Tank network dynamics and energy minimization for discrete combinatorial optimization.
Discuss modern adaptations including CRAM and pseudolikelihood estimation over discrete belief grids.
Analyze the critical distinction between structural constraint recovery and true reasoning dynamics.
Examine chain-of-thought reasoning capabilities and scaling behavior in frontier language models.
Review program-aided language models and code synthesis for deterministic constraint satisfaction problems.
Highlight failure modes in direct token-by-token backtracking search without external execution environments.
Define the Sudoku-Extreme problem setup: an 81-cell grid with 9 discrete states per cell and median 26 clues, treated with opaque indexing.
Specify Paradigm A: Direct LLM reasoning with adaptive thinking under high effort and a 32,000-token limit.
Specify Paradigm B: Programmatic solver generation, requesting a self-contained standard-library Python backtracking algorithm via a single zero-shot prompt.
Formalize the CRAM energy function over an 81x9 belief grid incorporating negative entropy, pairwise 9x9 couplings, and unary biases.
Detail the pseudolikelihood optimization objective implemented in NumPy on 1,000 solved training boards without GPU acceleration.
Formulate the hand-set energy baseline using Hopfield-Tank penalty rules parameterized by a single fixed scalar weight.
Describe the C-based focused Gibbs search inference procedure using 4 chains initialized from random boards and a 10 million move cutoff.
Detail the evaluation environment: Apple M4 Pro laptop CPU, zero GPU requirements, and total API expenditure of $3.75.
Describe the dataset partition: 500 test puzzles sampled from sapientinc/sudoku-extreme across 5 seeded random pages.
List evaluated model variants: Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Haiku 5.5 across direct solving and code synthesis conditions.
Define evaluation metrics: puzzle solve rate, incorrect board stops, token exhaustion rates, financial cost ($ per puzzle and $ per solved board), and execution wall-clock latency.

Report direct LLM reasoning performance: Opus 5.5 (3/5 solved, 2 token limit hits, $0.71/solved, 124.9s median), Sonnet 5.5 (3/5 solved, 2 token limit hits, $0.416/solved, 166.1s median), and Haiku 5.5 (3/10 solved, 5 token limit hits, 2 wrong answers with 74/81 and 78/81 cells correct).

Analyze LLM solver-writing performance: all 9 generated solvers (3 per model) solved 500/500 test puzzles (4,500/4,500 total solves) with 1.02-1.85 ms median execution latency at generation costs under $0.07.

Evaluate CRAM CPU performance: learned energy solves 496-497/500 across 3 seeds (fit time 2.51-2.52s, median latency 53.2-61.1 ms) with 0 wrong stops; hand-set energy matches it with 497/500 solves (0 fit time, 42.8 ms median latency).
Present direct 10-puzzle crossover: learned CRAM solved 10/10 puzzles including those that caused Opus and Sonnet to exceed token limits (solving them in 66 ms and 122 ms).
Analyze the learned coupling parameters of CRAM across 3 training seeds.
Demonstrate that for every cell, the top-20 learned same-digit interaction weights correspond exactly to its 20 true row, column, and box peers (peer recovery = 1.000).
Discuss why identical performance between hand-set and learned energies corroborates the hypothesis that Sudoku benchmarks measure local constraint satisfaction rather than high-order reasoning.
Reiterate that asking frontier LLMs to solve combinatorial constraint puzzles 'in their head' is uneconomical, slow, and error-prone.
Highlight that delegating combinatorial problem solving to prompt-generated deterministic code is orders of magnitude faster, cheaper, and 100% accurate.
Summarize the independent verification of CRAM on CPU, underscoring that hand-set energy parity reinforces the original authors' caution regarding benchmark reasoning claims.
Acknowledge the limited sample size (5-10 puzzles) for direct LLM solving due to API token cost constraints.
Note that the CRAM re-implementation is an independent CPU build rather than execution of the original author codebase.
Propose future investigations into harder NP-complete benchmarks where simple constraint graphs and deterministic backtracking solvers do not trivialise the search space.
